paragraphs.text: Last month the city council debated whether to make the 14 and 22 bus lines free for riders. Supporters packed the meeting, and so did a few business owners who were worried about the cost. This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate. I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not. Most mornings the bus is full before it reaches the hospital stop.

paragraphs.text: Fares are a bigger barrier than most people think, a monthly pass costs $64, which is more than many students spend on food in a week. A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once. My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all. When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up. People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers. Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change.

paragraphs.text: The main objection is cost. Fares pay for about a fifth of the system, and the city would have to replace that money from somewhere. This is a fair point, and I understand why people worry about it. Some council members said a small fee keeps riders respectful, I do not think that is true. Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude.

paragraphs.text: Free buses would also help the environment. More riders means fewer cars downtown and less traffic near the hospital, where ambulances get stuck every afternoon. On my route I count at least ten cars for every bus at the Grant Street light. The council's own report says the downtown streets are already over capacity at rush hour. Cleaner air matters to everyone who lives near Grant Street. Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.

item.text: Your one-year trial proposal is already in the conclusion. I’ll save a checklist that starts there and flags the two places Dr. Weiss wants evidence. I’ll also queue three grammar fixes for you to review, in line with your English 110 agreement.

items.text: Start with the one-year trial. Move your proposal for routes 14 and 22 from the conclusion to the introduction, in place of “This essay will look at both sides.” Which detail from your ride or your roommate’s walk best explains why you want the council to try it? Give that reason in your own words.

Check the source behind the Riverton example. Name it, give the ridership change and the period it covers, and explain what that comparison can tell the council about the 14 and 22. If you can’t verify the increase, drop the claim in both paragraphs 2 and 5 and develop the $64 pass example.

Answer the cost objection in paragraph 3. Check what the one-fifth figure covers. Use a city budget or council document to identify a plausible way to cover lost fares on the two routes, then explain what paying for the trial that way would cost the city. Check the meeting record before attributing “respectful” to council members. If that point takes you away from funding, cut it.

Reread paragraph 4 alongside your observation that the 22 is full before the hospital. What evidence shows that free fares would get drivers to switch to buses? Keep the traffic point if you can make that link. Decide whether to develop crowding as a cost of the trial in paragraph 3 or cut the last sentence.

Return to the one-year trial in the conclusion. What should the council look at after a year to decide whether to continue? The draft is about 390 words and the final calls for about 1,000. Use the extra space for your evidence and your answer on funding.
After revising, review the two comma-splice suggestions in paragraphs 2 and 3 and the subject–verb agreement suggestion in paragraph 4. Read the new material aloud once for the same patterns.

paragraphs.text: Last month the city council debated whether to make the 14 and 22 bus lines free for riders. Supporters packed the meeting, and so did a few business owners who were worried about the cost. This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate. I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not. Most mornings the bus is full before it reaches the hospital stop.

paragraphs.text: Fares are a bigger barrier than most people think, a monthly pass costs $64, which is more than many students spend on food in a week. A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once. My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all. When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up. People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers. Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change.

paragraphs.text: The main objection is cost. Fares pay for about a fifth of the system, and the city would have to replace that money from somewhere. This is a fair point, and I understand why people worry about it. Some council members said a small fee keeps riders respectful, I do not think that is true. Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude.

paragraphs.text: Free buses would also help the environment. More riders means fewer cars downtown and less traffic near the hospital, where ambulances get stuck every afternoon. On my route I count at least ten cars for every bus at the Grant Street light. The council's own report says the downtown streets are already over capacity at rush hour. Cleaner air matters to everyone who lives near Grant Street. Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.

Students, nurses and part-time workers would feel the difference first. I think the city should try free buses on the 14 and 22 for one year and count who rides. If ridership grows the way it did in Riverton, the council will have its answer.

items.text: Start with the one-year trial. Move your proposal for routes 14 and 22 from the conclusion to the introduction, in place of “This essay will look at both sides.” Which detail from your ride or your roommate’s walk best explains why you want the council to try it? Give that reason in your own words.

Check the source behind the Riverton example. Name it, give the ridership change and the period it covers, and explain what that comparison can tell the council about the 14 and 22. If you can’t verify the increase, drop the claim in both paragraphs 2 and 5 and develop the $64 pass example.

Answer the cost objection in paragraph 3. Check what the one-fifth figure covers. Use a city budget or council document to identify a plausible way to cover lost fares on the two routes, then explain what paying for the trial that way would cost the city. Check the meeting record before attributing “respectful” to council members. If that point takes you away from funding, cut it.

Reread paragraph 4 alongside your observation that the 22 is full before the hospital. What evidence shows that free fares would get drivers to switch to buses? Keep the traffic point if you can make that link. Decide whether to develop crowding as a cost of the trial in paragraph 3 or cut the last sentence.

Return to the one-year trial in the conclusion. What should the council look at after a year to decide whether to continue? The draft is about 390 words and the final calls for about 1,000. Use the extra space for your evidence and your answer on funding.
After revising, review the two comma-splice suggestions in paragraphs 2 and 3 and the subject–verb agreement suggestion in paragraph 4. Read the new material aloud once for the same patterns.

item.text:
I saved a revision checklist on your bus essay in Second Draft and added three grammar suggestions you can accept or reject.

When you get off work at nine, start by moving your one-year trial proposal for routes 14 and 22 from the conclusion to the opening. Your roommate’s forty-minute walk gives you a concrete way to explain why the trial matters.

The draft is about 390 words, and the final asks for about 1,000. Spend most of that extra space on two questions Dr. Weiss raised. How much did ridership rise in Riverton, and what source gives that figure? How would the city cover the lost fares during the trial? If you can’t verify the Riverton figure, the checklist points you back to the $64 pass and your roommate’s experience.

The essay is open for you to revise and submit by 11:59 p.m. tonight.
